Correlation Measures

Partial correlation: adjusting for another variable

Linear partial correlation measures the Pearson correlation between the residuals of x and y after regressing each on the same control variables. It ranges from -1 to +1 when both residual variances are nonzero. All data is synthetic. Back to the Notebook Gallery

1. Explore a shared influence

Generate z and independent noise terms, then set ||(x=az+\epsilon_x||) and ||(y=bx+az+\epsilon_y||). With b = 0, any population association between x and y comes from z. Compare the original observations with the residuals after adjusting for z.

data.text/markdown:
2. Formula and worked calculation

For one control variable z: ||[ r_{xy\cdot z}= \frac{r_{xy}-r_{xz}r_{yz}} {\sqrt{(1-r_{xz}^2)(1-r_{yz}^2)}}. ||]If all three pairwise correlations equal 0.8, the numerator is 0.8 - 0.64 = 0.16 and the denominator is sqrt(0.36 x 0.36) = 0.36. Thus partial r = 0.444, lower than the raw correlation of 0.8. For multiple controls, use the same residual approach with an intercept and all control columns in each regression. Perfectly explained x or y leaves zero residual variance and makes partial correlation undefined.

3. Estimation and interpretation

The residual calculation needs no normality assumption. Under an independent multivariate normal model with unknown mean and covariance, and a positive-definite sample covariance, sample partial correlation is the plug-in MLE of the population partial correlation. It is not generally unbiased in finite samples. Zero partial correlation is not generally conditional independence. That equivalence holds for multivariate normal variables, but nonlinear conditional relationships may remain in other distributions.

4. Limitations

Linear adjustment removes fitted linear components, not every possible influence of z. Nonlinearities, measurement error, and unmeasured variables can leave misleading results. Outliers and highly correlated controls can destabilize estimates. Controlling for a variable does not automatically remove causal bias. Conditioning on a collider can create association; adjusting for a mediator changes the causal question. Choose controls using subject knowledge, not just their observed correlations.

Try it yourself

  1. With b = 0, increase the shared influence. Compare raw and partial r.
  2. Set a = 0 and vary b. Why are the two correlations similar?
  3. Set b negative while a stays positive. Can adjustment reverse the sign?
  4. Explain why the direct coefficient b and partial r are not the same quantity.
